sources.debate_topic: Remember back in the days when you didn't have to argue about every damn thing? We all agreed that we'd landed on the Moon, that whatever Walter Cronkite said was true, and that OJ was a lovable scamp. Ok, maybe those days weren't so great. But at least there was a mainstream. Now we're all familiar with the dangers of mainstreams, but they do serve the useful purpose of providing a basic set of beliefs and values as a common ground. Or at least a way of writing off other opinions and outlooks. And investing majoritarian beliefs with explicit and implicit authority. So, yay for mainstreams? LLMs now provide us with a new mainstream, one grounded not in cultural “consensus” but in patterns discovered in enormous piles of text. One happy (?) result is that if you ask a major LLM if vaccines cause autism, they say no without equivocation and with justifications for their confidence.[1] If LLMs' power over the mainstream makes us uncomfortable, then how should LLMs handle it? Should they suss out the user's beliefs and values and always support them? Should they challenge every mainstream belief?
